content: At the time of the tuberculin skin tests (TSTs), the patient was undergoing treatment for her arthritis. After completing 12 months of therapy with second-line anti-tuberculosis (TB) medications, her medical condition showed significant improvement. Case 3: A 54-year-old woman, born in a country with a high prevalence of TB, was exposed to an individual with contagious TB in 1996. During the contact investigation, she tested positive on the TST but was not treated for latent TB infection (LTBI). The patient had a history of Crohn's disease and received infliximab infusions in February 2001 and June 2002. Two weeks after her second infusion, but 16 months after the first infusion, she presented with symptoms of cough, fever, and abdominal pain. A chest radiograph revealed upper-lobe lung nodules accompanied by a pleural effusion. Sputum specimens confirmed the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis. She was initiated on standard four-drug anti-TB therapy but experienced gastrointestinal intolerance. Consequently, isoniazid was discontinued, and she completed treatment with rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, achieving resolution of her TB disease. Additional Reports: In 2003, the California Department of Health Services requested local jurisdictions to report TB cases associated with tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) antagonists since January 2002. Among the reported cases, many patients were either born in countries with a high prevalence of TB or had known contact with individuals with active TB disease. Eight patients were concurrently receiving other immunosuppressive therapies at the time of their TB diagnoses. Only three patients underwent a medical history evaluation for TB risk factors before initiating therapy with a TNF-α antagonist. In addition to the patient described in Case 1, another patient died during TB treatment, with the cause of death attributed to cardiomyopathy. Editorial Note: As of January 2004, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) adverse event reporting system had received several hundred reports of TB disease in patients treated with TNF-α antagonists, most of which originated from outside the United States. Manufacturers of these products are required to report known cases of TB, but reporting by other sources remains voluntary. The majority of these cases likely represent the progression of LTBI to active TB disease, although the contribution of newly acquired Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection cannot be excluded.
